Look at the n_stations coefficient. Answer both questions in one or two sentences each:

β̂ reading: Can you tell the housing agency that bike share stations raise rents? Why or why not?
Your answer: No. This is an observational cross-section. Indego sites stations in dense, central, high-demand neighborhoods, so n_stations stands in for centrality and amenities the model doesn’t measure (omitted variables), and demand may drive station placement rather than the reverse. The coefficient is an association, not a causal effect.
ŷ reading: Should n_stations stay in a model whose only job is predicting rent? Why or why not?
Your answer: Yes, if it lowers out-of-sample error (check the CV RMSE in Part 6). The agency has station counts for every tract, the variable is not built from rent, and being a proxy for location desirability is exactly what makes it useful for prediction.







NoteSame number, two questions



If your answers to 1 and 2 differ, that’s the point. For inference, a variable that stands in for something unmeasured is a problem. For prediction, it can be exactly why the model works.

text:
Part 5: Uncertainty in input data
Our Y is an ACS estimate with its own margin of error. Add the residuals to the table and check whether the biggest misses happen where the estimate is least reliable.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(fitted_m2 = fitted(m2),
         resid_m2  = residuals(m2))

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = rent_cv, y = abs(resid_m2))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "CV of the median rent estimate (%)",
       y = "Size of the model's miss ($)",
       title = "Are the biggest misses in the noisiest tracts?") +
  theme_minimal()








Stop and look: If a tract’s rent estimate has a CV of 35%, how much of the model’s miss there could be survey noise rather than a model failure? What does that mean for flagging “tracts with rents above expectation”?

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 6: Fit vs. prediction






WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(5080)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[-train_idx, ]

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

   train     test 
252.9016 265.9391 


Stop and look: Which RMSE is larger? Why would you expect that? In words: “The model’s typical miss on tracts it hasn’t seen is about $266 per month.”
Change the seed to any other number and rerun the chunk. Did the test RMSE change? That’s why one split isn’t enough.


6B: 10-fold cross-validation
caret wants a plain data frame, so drop the geometry first. (The geometry isn’t a predictor, and train() will choke on it.)

model_df <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry()

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m1 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m2 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

Part 7: Where is the model wrong?

7A: Residuals vs. fitted

  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +

    studentized Breusch-Pagan test

data:  m2
BP = 13.662, df = 4, p-value = 0.008456


Stop and look: Random cloud, funnel, or curve? If it’s a funnel, the predictions aren’t biased, but one RMSE hides the fact that the model misses by much more in some tracts. Which tracts?


7B: The map
The residuals are already a column in an sf data frame. Mapping them is one geom_sf() away.

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_m2), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Where the rent model is wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = rent higher than predicted · Blue = lower than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")








Stop and look: If the errors were random, the map would look speckled. Does it? Where do the reds sit together? What might those places have in common that the model doesn’t know about?
Write down your answer. We’ll come back to it in Weeks 6 and 7.

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 8: The Challenge
Your team’s job: build the best model for predicting tract median rent, then use it to answer the agency’s question.

Rules

The grade is 10-fold CV RMSE. Use model_df (or tracts) and run set.seed(5080) directly before train(), exactly as in Part 6B, so every team is tested on the same folds.
Don’t drop rows. If you add a variable with missing values, you change the folds and the comparison stops being fair. Fill the gaps or choose a different variable.
You may add any ACS variables (use load_variables(2023, "acs5") to browse) and any spatial feature you can build with Week 4 tools: distances, buffers, counts.
You may not use anything built from rent itself. That rules out med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden (B25071), and the rent distribution tables (B25063). Ask yourself: would the agency have this variable for a tract whose rent it’s trying to predict? If not, using it is cheating the test. That’s called leakage.



Deliver

Your CV RMSE, in dollars, written as a sentence.
One feature you added, and why. What did you think it would capture that the census variables miss? Did it help?
One coefficient, read twice. Pick a variable in your final model and give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
The agency’s list. Using your final model fit to all tracts, find the five tracts with the largest positive residuals (rent well above expectation). For each, report the residual and the rent CV. Which of the five would you tell the agency to trust, and which might be fog?
Your residual map. Did your added features make the clusters from Part 7B shrink?


8.1 Extra ACS variables (none built from rent)

extra_acs <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(
    med_value   = "B25077_001",   # median value, owner-occupied units
    yr_built    = "B25035_001",   # median year structure built
    med_rooms   = "B25018_001",   # median number of rooms
    hu_total    = "B25002_001",   # housing units
    hu_vacant   = "B25002_003",   # vacant units
    pov_univ    = "B17001_001",   # poverty universe
    pov_below   = "B17001_002",   # below poverty
    workers     = "B08301_001",   # workers 16+
    transit     = "B08301_010",   # commute by public transit
    units_total = "B25024_001",   # units in structure: total
    u_1det      = "B25024_002",   # 1-unit detached
    u_1att      = "B25024_003",   # 1-unit attached (rowhomes)
    u_20_49     = "B25024_008",   # 20-49 units
    u_50plus    = "B25024_009",   # 50+ units
    med_age     = "B01002_001"    # median age
  ),
  year = 2023,
  output = "wide",
  geometry = FALSE
) %>%
  transmute(
    GEOID,
    med_value   = med_valueE,
    yr_built    = yr_builtE,
    med_rooms   = med_roomsE,
    pct_vacant  = hu_vacantE / hu_totalE * 100,
    pct_poverty = pov_belowE / pov_univE * 100,
    pct_transit = transitE / workersE * 100,
    pct_single  = (u_1detE + u_1attE) / units_totalE * 100,
    pct_bigbldg = (u_20_49E + u_50plusE) / units_totalE * 100,
    med_age     = med_ageE
  )



8.2 Spatial features (Week 4 tools)

city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_centroid(st_geometry(tracts))
nearest   <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts_ch <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    dist_ch_mi      = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)[, 1]) / 5280,
    dist_station_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest, ],
                                             by_element = TRUE)) / 5280
  ) %>%
  left_join(extra_acs, by = "GEOID")   # left_join keeps every row, in the same order



8.3 Fill the gaps; don’t drop rows (Rule 2)

impute_vars <- c("med_value", "yr_built", "med_rooms", "pct_vacant", "pct_poverty",
                 "pct_transit", "pct_single", "pct_bigbldg", "med_age")

# How many gaps are there before filling?
colSums(is.na(st_drop_geometry(tracts_ch)[impute_vars]))

tracts_ch <- tracts_ch %>%
  mutate(
    value_missing = as.integer(is.na(med_value)),   # flag tracts with no home-value estimate
    across(all_of(impute_vars), ~ if_else(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x))
  )

# Same rows, same order as Part 6B, so the folds are identical
stopifnot(nrow(tracts_ch) == nrow(tracts),
          identical(tracts_ch$GEOID, tracts$GEOID))

model_df_ch <- tracts_ch %>% st_drop_geometry()



8.4 Compare candidate models with 10-fold CV

f_base  <- med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations
f_value <- update(f_base, . ~ . + log(med_value) + value_missing)
f_a     <- med_rentE ~ log(med_incE) + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations +
             log(med_value) + value_missing + med_rooms + yr_built
f_b     <- update(f_a, . ~ . + pct_vacant + pct_poverty + pct_transit +
                    pct_single + pct_bigbldg + med_age +
                    log1p(dist_ch_mi) + log1p(dist_station_mi))

set.seed(5080)
cv_base  <- train(f_base,  data = model_df_ch, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
set.seed(5080)
cv_value <- train(f_value, data = model_df_ch, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
set.seed(5080)
cv_a     <- train(f_a,     data = model_df_ch, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
set.seed(5080)
cv_b     <- train(f_b,     data = model_df_ch, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

cv_results <- tibble(
  model = c("Base (m2)", "Base + home value", "A: + log income, housing stock",
            "B: A + neighborhood & location"),

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number published by the American Community Survey is an estimate based on a sample rather than a complete count. Each estimate therefore comes with a margin of error that describes its statistical uncertainty.
In this analysis, I examine median gross rent across counties in New York State and ask which communities are measured most and least reliably. Understanding the uncertainty in rent estimates is important because these data may influence housing policy and the allocation of affordable housing resources.

How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 100 dollars means something different for an estimate of 800 dollars than for an estimate of 2,000 dollars. To compare uncertainty across counties, I calculate the margin of error as a percentage of the estimate.

county_data <- county_data %>%

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To compare the reliability of the rent estimate with county population, I pull median gross rent and total population together in wide format.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York        1252     22  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York       754     33   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York         1436     11 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York         914     26  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York    759     30   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York         895     39   75464    NA


The E suffix identifies an estimate, while the M suffix identifies its margin of error. Therefore, myvarE and myvarM contain the median gross rent estimate and margin of error, while popE and popM contain the corresponding population values.

county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now I compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE, na.rm = TRUE)

# A tibble: 3 × 3

  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         51        381479.
2 Low confidence           1          5102 
3 Moderate                10         41178.


High-confidence counties have an average population of approximately 381,479, compared with approximately 41,178 in moderate-confidence counties. Hamilton County, the only low-confidence county, has an estimated population of 5,102. This pattern suggests that counties with smaller populations tend to have less precise median gross rent estimates. It is consistent with the smaller ACS samples generally available in less populated places.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The results show that Hamilton County is the New York county we know the least about for median gross rent. Its estimated median gross rent is $860, with a margin of error of $95, or about 11.0 percent of the estimate. It is the only county classified as low confidence under the thresholds used here. Schuyler and Greene Counties also have relatively large margins of error, at approximately 8.7 percent and 8.0 percent, respectively, and are classified as moderate confidence.
This pattern is related to the way the American Community Survey works. The ACS is based on a sample rather than a complete count of every household. Counties with smaller populations generally provide fewer sampled households, so their estimates tend to be less precise. In this analysis, high-confidence counties have an average population of about 381,479, compared with about 41,178 for moderate-confidence counties and 5,102 for the low-confidence county. These results are consistent with the expectation that smaller places are measured with greater uncertainty.
Ignoring this uncertainty could create unfair policy outcomes. If New York State allocated affordable-housing funds using median rent estimates alone, Hamilton County could be treated as though its estimate were just as precise as estimates for much larger counties. A county near a funding threshold might receive too little assistance, or be excluded entirely, because of sampling variation rather than a genuine difference in housing needs. Agencies should therefore consider both the estimate and its margin of error, especially when making decisions about small rural communities.

title: Verify the Claim: Lubrano, Alfred. “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty.”
text:
The article compares the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 American Community Survey (ACS) five-year estimates. I use B17001_002 for the estimated number of people below the poverty level and B17001_001 for the population whose poverty status was determined. Dividing the first estimate by the second gives a poverty rate. I use ACS five-year data because those are the periods identified in the article and tract-level data are available. The periods do not overlap: one ends in 2010 and the other begins in 2013.
The article reports figures for neighborhoods such as Eastwick and Fairhill but does not identify which census tracts it assigned to each neighborhood. I therefore analyze Philadelphia census tracts. I assume the same ACS poverty definition can be used in both periods. My tract results describe geographic patterns in the city; they cannot reproduce the article’s exact neighborhood estimates.

    county = "Philadelphia",
    year = yr,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide"
  ) %>%
    mutate(period = paste0(yr - 4, "-", yr))
}

poverty_2017 <- get_poverty(2017)

text:
Part 2 — Test
For each tract, I calculate the poverty rate and use moe_prop() to calculate the margin of error (MOE) of that rate. The MOE of the poverty count cannot simply be used as the MOE of the rate. I then calculate the coefficient of variation (CV) from the rate’s standard error. I classify CV values below 12% as reliable, 12%–40% as somewhat reliable, and above 40% as unreliable.


Show code
calculate_rate <- function(data) {
  data %>%
    mutate(
      rate = case_when(
        totalE > 0 ~ belowE / totalE,
        TRUE ~ NA_real_
      ),
      rate_moe = case_when(
        totalE > 0 ~ moe_prop(belowE, totalE, belowM, totalM),
        TRUE ~ NA_real_
      ),
      cv = case_when(
        rate > 0 ~ (rate_moe / 1.645) / rate * 100,
        TRUE ~ NA_real_
      ),
      reliability = case_when(
        is.na(cv) ~ "Unavailable",
        cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
        cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
        TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
      )
    )
}

poverty_2010 <- calculate_rate(poverty_2010)
poverty_2017 <- calculate_rate(poverty_2017)

poverty_2017 %>%
  count(reliability)

2 Somewhat reliable   332
3 Unavailable           8
4 Unreliable           22


The two periods contain 384 tracts each. In 2013–2017, 22 tract estimates are reliable under the CV rule, 332 are somewhat reliable, 22 are unreliable, and 8 have no calculable rate.


Show code

    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z = change / se_diff,

title: Verify the Claim: Lubrano, Alfred. “New Census figures on Philly neighborhoods show inequality, high numbers of whites living in poverty.”
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate
Supported. The article describes Philadelphia’s 2013–2017 poverty rate as approximately 26%. A separate ACS estimate for Philadelphia County is 25.8%, which rounds to 26%. The tract results also show that poverty rates increased in some parts of the city: 36 tracts show an increase at the 90% confidence level.
Not supported by this test. A broad reading that poverty rose dramatically across Philadelphia as a whole goes further than these tract results show. Only 36 of 376 comparable tracts show a detectable increase; 27 show a detectable decrease, and 313 show no detectable change. This does not disprove an increase in any particular neighborhood.
Cannot be determined: The article’s exact figures for Eastwick, Fairhill, and Holmesburg cannot be checked with this tract analysis because the article does not provide its tract-to-neighborhood boundaries. Its claim about white poverty also requires race-specific data, which the overall poverty variables do not measure.

Part 4 — Rewrite
Philadelphia’s 2013–2017 ACS puts the city’s poverty rate at about 26%. Across its census tracts, the pattern of change is mixed. I test every model with the helper below. It splits the tracts into 10 groups, trains the model on 9 of them, and checks how far off it is on the 10th, repeating this 10 times. It uses the same split every time, so all models are tested fairly. It also stops if a variable has missing values, so no tracts are dropped by mistake.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection
My baseline model was off by about 13.4 percentage points on tracts it had not seen. The final model lowers this to 13.0, a small improvement of about 0.4 points. What surprised me most was that the spatial features barely helped. Burglary density was the only one that helped a little, maybe because burglaries are more common where homes are packed closely together. The most disappointing was distance to the nearest campus, which made the model worse. The campus file has many small buildings across the city, and age and education already capture students. Most of the improvement came from reshaping the variables instead: taking logs and letting the distance to City Hall curve. I learned that a variable can look useful on a map but add little once similar variables are already in the model.
Take median age. The β̂ reading: if two tracts are the same in every other way, the one whose median age is 10 years older is predicted to have about 9.4 percentage points fewer renters (the coefficient is −0.94 per year). This shows a relationship, not a cause; getting older does not by itself make people buy homes. The ŷ reading: median age stays in the model because it helps predict the renter share more accurately, whether or not it is a cause.
The final map still shows clusters in Manayunk, Roxborough, and parts of the lower Northeast, where there are more renters than predicted. Next, I would add the age and size of buildings from the Office of Property Assessment, because old rowhouses split into apartments are often rented even where incomes are moderate. I would also add college enrollment from the Census (table B14007) to tell students apart from long-term renters.
The last plot shows that the size of the error has almost nothing to do with how reliable the estimate is. Big errors happen at every CV level, and the correlation is only about 0.06. Still, for about 60% of tracts, the model’s error is smaller than the estimate’s own margin of error, so in those tracts the error could just be survey noise. But the biggest errors seem to come from the model missing something, not from noisy data.

check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}

Answer: What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?
Your answer: Four things shaped our plan. First, prices are strongly right-skewed: the median cleaned sale is $300,000 but the mean is about $430,000, with a long tail into the millions. Rule 4 keeps the outcome in dollars, so RMSE will be driven by the expensive houses, and we expect our biggest misses there. We can’t log the outcome, but we can log skewed predictors. Second, the flexible curves for building size and building age do not follow the straight lines, so we will test log() and squared (I(x^2)) terms and keep them only if CV RMSE improves. Third, the price map shows that prices cluster by place. A structure-only model will leave spatially clustered errors, and Rule 5 bars features built from neighbors’ prices, so we will build location features from open data: tract characteristics from the ACS, distances to amenities, crime exposure (buffer counts and kNN distances), and neighborhood fixed effects. Fourth, the median price rose from $283,000 in 2023 to $310,000 in 2024 and $321,900 in 2025, so sale year and quarter belong in the model as categories.

title: A Nightmare in Regression Class
text:
4 Part 2: Build the model
Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns model, added, cv_rmse, moran_i, notes.
Every model is scored the same way: 10-fold CV RMSE on the same folds (the provided cv_rmse()), and global Moran’s I of the out-of-fold residuals, using each house’s 5 nearest training sales as neighbors. Residual = actual − predicted, so a positive residual means the model guessed too low. A falling Moran’s I means the errors are clustering less in space.
Rule check for every feature below: nothing is built from a sale price. The Assessor could compute every one of them for a house that did not sell.

4.1 Scoring helpers and the model log


Reveal the Code
# Spatial weights: each training house's 5 nearest training sales
w_knn <- nb2listw(knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(train), k = 5)), style = "W")

# Global Moran's I of a residual vector
moran_of <- function(resid) as.numeric(moran.mc(resid, w_knn, nsim = 499)$statistic)

# Score one formula: CV RMSE, out-of-fold residuals, Moran's I
score_model <- function(f) {
  resid <- train$sale_price - cv_pred(f, train)
  list(cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f, train),
       moran_i = moran_of(resid),
       resid   = resid)
}

model_log <- tibble(model = character(), added = character(),
                    cv_rmse = numeric(), moran_i = numeric(), notes = character())
resids <- list()   # out-of-fold residuals of every model, for the Part 3 maps




4.2 M1: Structure-only baseline
Every house feature in the file. fireplace_missing is the flag from Part 1.


Reveal the Code
f1 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + lotsize_acre + building_age +
  num_bedrooms + num_full_baths + num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + fireplace_missing +
  garage_size + central_air + one_story + full_basement + finished_basement +
  brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace

s1 <- score_model(f1)
resids$m1 <- s1$resid
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m1", added = "structure only (baseline)",
          cv_rmse = s1$cv_rmse, moran_i = s1$moran_i,
          notes = "Required baseline: what the house alone can tell us, before any location.")
model_log

4.3 M2: The shape of building size and lot size
In Part 1, the flexible curve for building size did not follow the straight line. We try three shapes and let CV RMSE choose.

                     f    = list(f1, f1_log, f1_sq)) %>%
  mutate(cv_rmse = map_dbl(f, ~ cv_rmse(.x, train))) %>%

resids$m2 <- s2$resid

          cv_rmse = s2$cv_rmse, moran_i = s2$moran_i,
          notes = "Part 1 scatter bent away from the straight line; compared linear, log and squared size.")




4.4 M3: A squared term for building age
The age curve in Part 1 was not a straight line either. Old Chicago houses (greystones, Victorians) can sell for more than mid-century ones, so value may fall with age and then rise again.


Reveal the Code
f3 <- update(f2, . ~ . + I(building_age^2))

s3 <- score_model(f3)
resids$m3 <- s3$resid
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", added = "+ building_age^2",
          cv_rmse = s3$cv_rmse, moran_i = s3$moran_i,
          notes = "Age curve bent in Part 1; a squared term lets the line turn.")

# Where does the age curve turn? Is it inside the data?
m3_fit <- lm(f3, data = st_drop_geometry(train))
b1 <- coef(m3_fit)["building_age"]
b2 <- coef(m3_fit)["I(building_age^2)"]
c(turning_point = unname(-b1 / (2 * b2)),
  min_age = min(train$building_age), max_age = max(train$building_age))

4.5 M4: Sale year and quarter as categories
Median prices rose each year (Part 1), and sales may differ by season. Year and quarter are labels, not amounts, so we make them factors. The reference level is 2023, Q1.


Reveal the Code

          cv_rmse = s4$cv_rmse, moran_i = s4$moran_i,
          notes = "Median price rose 2023 to 2025 (Part 1); prices also move with season.")




4.6 M5: Distance to the Loop and to the nearest ‘L’ station
The price map in Part 1 shows prices clustering by place. The first two location features: distance to the Loop (City Hall), and distance to the nearest CTA ‘L’ stop (Chicago Data Portal, dataset 8pix-ypme). We log both distances, because moving from 500 to 2,500 ft from a station matters more than moving from 20,000 to 22,000 ft.

                                          by_element = TRUE))

4.7 M6: Exposure to violent crime
Violent crime is a disamenity a buyer cares about and the house file can’t see. We pull robberies, homicides, aggravated assaults and aggravated batteries for 2023–2025 (FBI codes 01A, 03, 04A, 04B) from the Chicago Data Portal (ijzp-q8t2). Then we build the three ways of operationalizing “near”, plus a logged kNN distance, and let CV RMSE pick one.

4.8 M7: Neighborhood characteristics from the Census
Houses in tracts with higher incomes, more college graduates and fewer vacant homes should sell for more, even after distance and crime. We take 2019–2023 ACS 5-year estimates for Cook County tracts and give each house the values of the tract it sits in. Income is skewed, so we log it. A few tracts have no estimate; we fill those with the training median and keep every row (Rule 1).

  geography = "tract", state = "IL", county = "Cook", year = 2023, survey = "acs5",
  variables = c(med_inc   = "B19013_001",   # median household income

Chicago’s 77 community areas each carry things we did not measure: reputation, schools, lake access, history. A fixed effect lets every area have its own intercept. Boundaries come from the Chicago Data Portal (igwz-8jzy).

6.1 4A. Where does the model fail worst?
Our final model (M8) has the largest mean absolute prediction errors in Lincoln Park ($504,283), Near North Side ($424,419), and Lake View ($322,603). These neighborhoods contain properties with substantial price variation, which may not be fully captured by our predictors.
In Lincoln Park, the model slightly underpredicts sale prices on average, with a mean residual of +$3,451. In Near North Side and Lake View, it slightly overpredicts prices, with mean residuals of -$1,322 and -$1,127, respectively. However, these average errors are relatively small compared with the mean absolute errors, suggesting that large overpredictions and underpredictions often cancel each other out.
This shows that community area fixed effects helped improve our model, but they cannot fully capture differences between individual properties, especially in neighborhoods with expensive and diverse housing markets.


6.2 4B. Does the assessment ratio differ by neighborhood income?
Yes. The median predicted-to-actual sale price ratio increases across neighborhood income groups, from 0.971 in the lowest-income neighborhoods to approximately 1.016 in the highest-income neighborhoods. The middle-income groups have median ratios of 0.987 and 0.995.
This suggests that our model slightly underpredicts home values in lower-income neighborhoods and slightly overpredicts values in higher-income neighborhoods. At the median, this is different from the regressive assessment pattern discussed in The Tax Divide, where lower-income homeowners face a disproportionate tax burden.
However, the mean assessment ratios are above 1 across all income groups, with the largest mean ratio in the lowest-income group (1.31). This indicates that some properties experience substantial overprediction, even when the median suggests underprediction. The difference between the mean and median is important when evaluating potential assessment inequities.
Our Part 1 cleaning rules excluded multi-parcel sales and transactions below $20,000. While these rules helped remove unusual transactions, they may also affect which properties are represented in our analysis, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods.
Finally, these are predictions from our model, not actual property tax assessments. Therefore, we cannot conclude that our model produces the same tax inequities described in The Tax Divide. However, the differences across income groups suggest that fairness should be evaluated carefully before using this type of model for property assessment.

8 Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

8.1 1. Reading a Coefficient Twice
In our final model (M8), the coefficient for building_000sf is approximately 175,638.8. Statistically, this means that a one-unit increase in building size, equivalent to 1,000 square feet, is associated with a $175,638.80 increase in predicted sale price, holding all other variables constant.
From a prediction perspective, if two houses have identical characteristics except that one is 1,000 square feet larger, our model predicts that the larger house will sell for approximately $175,639 more. This illustrates how structural characteristics directly influence the model’s estimated property values.


8.2 2. Would We Recommend This Model to the Assessor?
We would recommend Model 8 as a useful starting point, but not as a fully automated assessment system. Our final cross-validation RMSE was $196,561.80, a substantial improvement over the baseline model. Adding neighborhood fixed effects, census characteristics, crime exposure, and accessibility measures helped capture important differences across Chicago.
However, the model still has limitations. The largest mean absolute errors occurred in Lincoln Park ($504,283), Near North Side ($424,419), and Lake View ($322,603). These neighborhoods may contain expensive or unusual properties that are difficult to predict accurately.
We also found differences in assessment ratios across neighborhood income groups. The median ratio increased from 0.971 in the lowest-income areas to 1.020 in the highest-income areas. Although this pattern differs from the regressive assessment problem described in The Tax Divide, it demonstrates why prediction accuracy and equity should be evaluated together.
Before using the model for taxation, we would recommend additional validation, reviewing unusual properties, checking the timing of external data, and regularly monitoring neighborhood-level errors.
